title: Prompt Injection attack against LLM-integrated Applications

object.carrier: Developer pre-designed (system) prompts of LLM-integrated applications: standing instructions fixed by the service provider, shared unchanged across all users and sessions, that the attack overrides in-context (prompt injection) and exfiltrates (prompt leaking).

safety_property.statement: An LLM-integrated application must (integrity) generate outputs serving only the functionality defined by the developer's pre-designed prompt, and (confidentiality) must not disclose that pre-designed prompt or let arbitrary users consume the provider's LLM computation for free. The property fails, in the authors' black-box setting, when a crafted user input makes the application execute an adversary-chosen command (content manipulation, code generation, spam generation, information gathering, prompt abuse) or repeat its original prompt (prompt leaking).
safety_property.operationalized_as: An application is counted vulnerable if any of five exploit scenarios (prompt leaking, code generation, content manipulation, spam generation, information gathering; Table 3 prompts) succeeds at least once, with each exploit prompt executed five times and outcomes manually verified (Table 4); server errors incited by injection are explicitly not counted as success.

capabilities: Black-box access to the target LLM-integrated application through its publicly accessible service endpoint and documentation
Freedom to arbitrarily manipulate the inputs provided to the application
Use of an auxiliary LLM (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo) to infer the application's internal context from observed input-output pairs
Automatic generation and feedback-driven iterative refinement of injected prompts based on application responses
assumptions: The adversary has no direct access to application internals such as the specific pre-constructed prompts, application structure, or the backend LLM
The adversary can only infer information from the responses generated by the service
Each exploit prompt is executed five times and success is manually verified by the authors
Server errors caused by prompt injection do not count as successful exploits
not_covered: Exploiting other application vulnerabilities such as front-end flaws
Poisoning external resources queried by the application to fulfill its tasks (indirect prompt injection from Internet content)
White-box or insider access to prompts, application structure, or backend models

intervention.name: HouYi (black-box prompt injection attack methodology)
intervention.description: An LLM-driven attack that first infers the target application's internal context from documentation and input-output pairs, then composes a three-part injected prompt: a Framework Component that blends with the application's normal flow and format, a Separator Component that forces context separation between the pre-designed prompt and user input (via syntax-based, language-switching, or semantic strategies), and a Disruptor Component carrying the malicious question; a feedback loop iteratively refines the components until the injection succeeds.

controls.name: Existing prompt injection techniques from prior work (direct injection, escape characters, context ignoring)

results.claim: Under the authors' evaluation setup, HouYi achieves an 86.1% application-level attack success rate: 31 of 36 real-world LLM-integrated applications are susceptible to black-box prompt injection.
results.setting: 36 real-world LLM-integrated applications selected from Supertools (10 pilot-study apps plus 26 additional); black-box access via public endpoints; attacker-side LLM GPT-3.5-turbo with temperature=1 and top_p=1; five exploit scenarios (prompt leaking, code generation, content manipulation, spam generation, information gathering); each exploit prompt executed five times; success manually verified.
results.quote: We develop our methodology into a toolkit and assess it across 36 LLM-integrated applications. The toolkit exhibits a high success rate of 86.1% in purloining the original prompt and/or utilizing the computational power across services

denominator.how_counted: 31 of the 36 evaluated applications deemed vulnerable; per §6.1 the authors 'designate an LLM-integrated application as vulnerable if prompt injection can be effectively executed on it', execute each exploit prompt five times, and manually verify each result (Table 4).

results.claim: HouYi's scan identified 31 unique vulnerabilities, of which 10 were confirmed and acknowledged by the vendors (including Notion and WriteSonic).
results.setting: Same 36-application evaluation; responsible disclosure to all evaluated applications; only vendors that acknowledged the findings permitted public naming (Notion, Parea, WriteSonic).
results.quote: Our approach has led to the successful identification of 31 unique vulnerabilities across a variety of applications. 10 have been confirmed and acknowledged by the vendors.

results.claim: Baseline contrast: existing heuristic prompt injection techniques achieved only partially successful exploits on two out of ten commercial LLM-integrated applications in the pilot study, motivating HouYi.
results.value: two of ten applications (partial exploits only; no full success)
results.setting: 10 commercial LLM-integrated applications from Supertools (two per category across five categories: chatbot, writing assistant, code assistant, business analysis, creative generation); three existing attack strategies (direct injection, escape characters, context ignoring) crossed with three malicious questions; each attack repeated five times (Table 1).
results.quote: We implement existing prompt injection techniques [20, 44, 6] on them, and only achieve partially successful exploits on two out of the ten targets.

denominator.how_counted: 10 commercial applications selected from Supertools; each prompt injection attack repeated five times and success rate recorded (Table 1).

results.claim: Prompt-abuse impact extrapolation: a free LLM-integrated application (Parea) could suffer an estimated $259.2 daily financial loss from attackers consuming its LLM budget.
results.setting: Parea AI prompt-optimization application; extrapolated (not an executed attack at scale) from 90k tokens processed per minute at GPT3.5-turbo pricing of $0.002 per 1k tokens over 1440 minutes; the authors confined experiments to avert real-world damage.
results.quote: our evaluation shows an alarming daily financial loss for Parea developers of $259.2, a figure derived from 90k tokens processed per minute [5] at a cost of $0.002 per 1k tokens using GPT3.5-turbo [45], extrapolated over 1440 minutes.

results.claim: Defense evaluation (qualitative): all six empirically proposed defenses the authors implemented (Instruction Defense, Post-Prompting, Random Sequence Enclosure, Sandwich Defense, XML Tagging, Separate LLM Evaluation) could be circumvented by HouYi in their manual evaluation; no numeric bypass rates are reported.
results.value: all evaluated defenses circumvented (qualitative, no numeric rate reported)
results.setting: Common defensive mechanisms applied to open-source LLM-integrated projects; outcomes judged through the authors' manual inspection; success rates for this defense evaluation are not quantified.
results.quote: In our evaluation, we have implemented and evaluated each of these defense strategies using HouYi. Through our manual inspection, we have found that HouYi can effectively circumvent these security measures

limitations.statement: Detected vulnerabilities may become non-reproducible over time as vendors deploy prompt injection protection or backend LLMs evolve, so the reported exploits can be transient.
limitations.quote: Given the swift evolution of LLM-integrated applications, certain detected vulnerabilities may become non-reproducible over time.

limitations.statement: The black-box setting precludes verifying whether an extracted prompt output is factual or LLM hallucination; the authors instead confirm findings with the service providers.
limitations.quote: This uncertainty arises from our black-box setting, which precludes us from verifying whether the output is factual or simply LLM-generated hallucination.

limitations.statement: In the pilot study the authors did not verify whether a printed prompt is correct or hallucinated, only whether the output deviated from the application's intended functionality.
limitations.quote: As our primary goal is to ascertain whether the prompt injection strategy could influence the model’s output, we does not specifically verify if the printed prompt is correct or hallucinated.
